He wants the Soviet Union type of efficiency.
Madam Speaker, on a separate topic, I wonder if the Government House Leader could either affirm or deny-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order, please. I believe I have a point of order on this topic.

Madam Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I am trying to assist the Government House Leader, as always, in the course of Government activity, and it is in that spirit that I rise. In order for us to make an assessment with respect to the amount of debating time that may be necessary on any piece of legislation, it seems to us in the Opposition that the common courtesy would be for the Government House Leader
to get up and give us an indication as to whether or not a decision has been made as to when the Speech from the Throne for the next session will be brought down.
The one they said is ready.

Maybe the one that is ready now, and has been for some months, if not years. That would be very helpful.

speechtext: Madam Speaker, I can assure the Hon. Member that if this session has been the longest in history it also has been, and is, the most important and the most productive.
Hear, hear!
Producing two million unemployed.

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: In almost three years we have succeeded in adopting over 150 Bills. We have not completed three years yet but already we have adopted over 150 Bills. We have patriated the Constitution; we have a new Charter of Rights; we have a National Energy Policy-
Oh, oh!

speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: -we have had two economic statements. This is and has been the most important and the most productive session ever.

speakerposition: Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext: The country is bankrupt.

speechtext:
The Hon. Member wants to know when is the next Speech from the Throne or when shall we stop dealing with the economy and start an eight-day debate, generally speaking. It has been made very clear under the parliamentary reform with which we are experimenting. I had to make a statement at the beginning of this semester, in January. The letter was made public, was sent to the House Leaders of both opposite Parties. This contained a list of all the Bills that have to be completed before we consider proroguing. With good will we could complete all the remaining stages of the important Bills. All this could be completed easily, with good will, within the next 15 days or so.
However, if there is no good will it could take longer, if the Opposition keeps forcing the Government to limit debate. We are under negotiation. If we do not achieve the results that we
March 10, 1983

speechtext: Pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 58, I do now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole.
The House resumed consideration in Committee of Bill C-139, to amend the Statute Law relating to Income Tax (No. 2)-Mr. Lalonde-Mr. Blaker in the Chair.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
When the House rose at one o'clock, the Committee of the Whole was considering Clause 4 and a series of associated Clauses and Subclauses. If my recollection
March 10, 1983

serves me correctly, the Hon. Member for Mississauga South had the floor.

Mr. Chairman, prior to lunch we got into the question of certain money funds that were organized and have been organized principally since the budget of November 12, 1981, making it possible for Canadians to invest in Canadian Government bonds and other Canadian Government securities in such a fashion that the funds can accumulate, accumulate and accumulate and there will be no accrual of tax. The various offerings in these funds were being peddled in the Toronto area and indeed across Canada. For reference this afternoon, I want to put on the record the detail of a company called "The Money Fund Limited".
The Money Fund is organized as a fund to invest in the medium-term debt obligations issued or guaranteed by Canada or a Province of Canada or an agent thereof in any financial institutions having a Standard and Poors rating of AAA. The question is asked in their prospectus which has been approved, issued by Bache Halsey Stuart Canada Ltd, 170 Laurier Avenue in Ottawa: "Why is an investment in a Money Fund tax-sheltered?" The answer is: "A Canadian resident investor will not be taxed on an accrual basis or have taxes payable in Canada or Nassau until such time as the B shares are redeemed".
The next question is: "Will an investor be liable for any taxes on the redemption of First Series A shares". The answer is: "No, there are no taxes payable by an investor upon redemption of the shares".
On the question of their B shares, they say: "All of the investment growth will be attributable to B series shares. The value of the shares will be subject to tax on the capital gain realized on any redemption of the series B shares".
The next question is: "Can this investment be used as bank collateral?" Here is the answer: "Yes. Bank of America Trust and Banking Corporation Bahamas Limited will normally provide excellent collateral loan facilities with shares of the Money Fund as collateral. The interest on the loan may be tax deductible as an expense to the investor."
That particular fund is open to any investor who wants to put $100,000 into it. In effect, the investor puts up $100,000. The fund issues him Series A shares, annually the interest which is payable and collectible in the Bahamas on Government of Canada securities, which by the way have no withholding tax on them, if received by the trust company in Bahamas. In place of giving the Canadian shareholder his interest on his share of the income received on the bond, the Canadian receives a Series B share. That Series B share can be redeemed at any time. It is totally open. Indeed, the Series A share in the fund is totally open and redeemable at any time.
The Series A share redeemable without cost because that is the original capital. The Series B share comes back to the Canadian subject to Canadian capital gains tax only because, after all, it is a share. In other words, there is no tax on the accumulation principle for money taken out of Canada and invested with these people. These people are able to and have
Income Tax
cleared their share issue with the Securities Commission of Ontario. The opinions with respect to the legality and the tax position on these securities has been cleared by the top solicitors in the country, indeed with the tax Department, if my memory serves me correctly.
This morning there was mention of the Casuarina Corporation. The Minister says that was six years ago. May 1 point out to him that the confidential offering memorandum for Casuarina is dated May 3, 1982. I pointed out this morning that Casuarina has already pulled out of Canada $80 million of investment funds that would have gone to mutual insurance companies in Canada. They would have been used in Canada for long-term mortgage investment in this country. The money was pulled out of Canada because of the nature of the income tax amendment now before us. There can be no justification whatsoever for this kind of activity that is allowed to take place, yet the very nature of the amendments before us initiate this activity and force money out of the country.
The Minister said privately before lunch that he had a legal opinion that people who went into these kind of schemes and invested in annuities or in these money funds outside of Canada may be avoiding Canadian income tax. I challenge him to present to this Committee that opinion. If he cannot produce that opinion, then he should withdraw all of these Clauses because these Clauses deliberately cause headaches and problems for Canadians. They take away the investment potential of Canada. They take money out of Canada and put it in foreign countries. That is what this income tax amendment and this part of the Section does. This Government does not realize what is happening.
This morning the Minister talked about the history of the annuity business in Canada. He was quite right. We were developing a very good deferred annuity business in this country where trust and insurance companies would take money in on long-term deposits and the interest would accumulate. That money was available for long-term mortgages and industrial bonds. What this Clause does is to force money invested in Canada by Canadians into short-term investment. It shortens the length of debt securities. It destabilizes the investment climate of the country. This particular series of Clauses is doing more harm to the investment climate of this country than any other series of Clauses in this horrendous set of amendments.
Has the Minister any current figures on the current attitude of Canadians toward buying deferred annuities since December 1, 1982? Have any Canadians bought them?

Mr. Chairman, I indicated before the one o'clock break that the issue the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has just characterized is generally known, I am told, as offshore mutual funds. It is likely that there are not a large number of Canadians knowledgeable of, or who have come in contact with, this provision. As the Hon. Member indicates,

March 10, 1983
Income Tax
they require the services of the highest price lawyers in Canada to set up the trust and give opinions on the matter. I for one have not had a reason to call upon such highpriced opinions or help. Obviously the majority of Canadians have not done so as well. It is probable, Mr. Chairman, that these Canadians who, because of their financial resources are able to call upon the best and most expensive advice on the conduct of their financial affairs must be first, the envy of some other Canadians, and second, I would think that some Canadians must feel a little frustrated, even a little angered, at the fact that there are some high rollers who have the resources necessary to take special advantage of the tax system.
However, getting back to the offshore mutual funds issue, it is not an offshore mutual annuity question; it is an offshore mutual fund tax technique.
So what?

The Hon. Member says, "so what?". The answer is that this special tax treatment has been in place for a number of years. It has nothing to do with this budget or specifically with annuities. It is only that annuities may be one of the riders under the trust, the mutual fund vehicle, that the issue now comes up. So I contest his protestation that this vehicle is the result of any of the Clauses which are before Parliament today on this issue.
That is some answer.

Some answer, as my friend says. The Minister says it is only the high rollers. Let me tell him that in the Casuarina prospectus the per unit cost is $10,000, not a great deal of money bearing in mind that the maximum amount of Canada Savings Bonds purchased by one individual is $35,000. If the Minister wants to buy the Money Fund, he can go down to Bache here in Ottawa and buy it. No problem, he does not have to be a high roller there. The Casuarina fund is financed and organized by the Royal Bank of Canada, not exactly an unknown institution in Canada. I am sure that if he really wanted to get involved he would just have to see his local Royal Bank manager, and that could be organized for him. The Minister says that is not an annuity, that is a money fund. Well, I want to point out that these Clauses deal with any investment situation where the money is invested and interest accumulates. The normal tax treatment in every jurisdiction in the world, other than this one if this Bill passes, is that interest is not taxable until it is received by the lender. Whether it is an annuity, an insurance policy, a guaranteed investment certificate or Canada Savings Bond with a cumulative feature, does not matter one iota.
The principle, Mr. Chairman, is that this Government wants to tax interest which has not been received. If people are going to save money in this fashion, they are going to earn a lot of money, and the Government says it is not going to get its tax fast enough. So the Government says, "Let us wring the neck of the golden goose; we will get the eggs out faster that way". I want to tell the Minister that he has wrung the neck of the golden goose. He has not answered my question about the
experience on the sale of deferred annuities since the beginning of December, 1982.

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member urges the Government not to take any leadership in drafting a tax system which we promote on the basis of equitable treatment of all Canadians. Yet scarcely a day goes by in the House that we are not urged by Hon. Members opposite that we do need specifically Canadian designed policies in, you name it, energy, housing, or interest rates. Then, because the Government of Canada takes leadership in proposing an equitable system for the vast majority of Canadian taxpayers, he complains that we are taking leadership. I do not know where the consistency is in that.
To make the observation that investment in annuities is down, as I indicated this morning, what does that add to our understanding of what has happened in the economy? Can you name six sectors of the economy which have shown improvement, or where financial investments have not suffered as a result of the downturn in the economy in the last 24 months? I doubt it.

The Minister still refuses to tell the House how much the sale of deferred annuities has decreased in the country since the Minister decided to bring in Subclauses 4(6) to (11). The money funds that I spoke of were deliberately set up to avoid the problems created for investors in those Clauses, the ones we are now dealing with.
The Minister said that the annuity business was great in Canada. That is what he said before lunch. I asked him what has happened to the sale of deferred annuities since December 1, 1982? He weaseled, he did not answer. I am going to sit down and expect an answer from him because he should have an answer and he should have it now.

Mr. Chairman, I am going to repeat the answer that I gave before the break, and the one which I just gave a few moments ago, that the sale of annuities is down.
If the Hon. Member for Mississauga South is so familiar with this fantastic tax scheme that permits people to have a tax advantage by getting high priced assistance-he has mentioned the name of McLeod, Young and Weir-I suspect he could get specific information on that question from the people who are offering those schemes. 1 have not been into the offices of McLeod, Young and Weir recently, but the Hon. Member has. I am sure they could give him that information.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The time allotted to the Hon. Member for Mississauga South has expired. The Chair recognizes the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North.

Mr. Chairman, I rise to make a plea to Members of the Official Opposition to let the House get on with its business. Millions of Canadians whose only income comes from wages or salaries, do not have money to squirrel away in an annuity or RRSP or any of the hundreds of loopholes which the tax laws provide so that people with money can
March 10, 1983

avoid paying taxes. I wish we could get off these pleas which we have heard all day for more concessions and more loopholes for people who already have more than enough.
I should like to discuss the problems of the people who cannot save money and those who can save a little but cannot afford the high-priced lawyers and accountants who give advice to people with money on how to avoid paying taxes.
Organizations such as the National Council on Welfare have documented evidence that large numbers of people in this country get away with paying little or no tax because of the loopholes in the tax laws. In 1978, approximately 2,316 people with assessed incomes of more than $50,000 did not pay any tax at all and 96 of them had incomes exceeding $200,000. In 1979 the Government lost more than $30 billion in revenue as a result of tax loopholes.
I wish we were not spending our time discussing ways to find more tax loopholes, which is what my friends from the Conservative Party are trying to do, but instead discussed ways to plug loopholes. People with money should pay their fair share of taxes and thus lighten the burden on people on low and middle incomes who do not have the money to invest or hide and who pay more tax than they should because they do not know how to avoid it.

Mr. Chairman, I am glad that the NDP has joined the debate. I think that Members of that Party are missing the point. What we are concerned about is the small Canadian who is being hurt by particular parts of this tax Bill. If the Hon. Member listens carefully perhaps we can identify some of those areas for him.
May I ask the Minister to reconsider the issue of court ordered asset splitting in relation to matrimonial matters. He knows that quite often in the process of a divorce, the courts order the splitting of assets. The Minister indicated that if the law remained as it is, then at the moment of divorce those people will be liable for increased taxation. This comes at a time when they can least afford it, financially or emotionally.
Has the Minister reconsidered my request for an amendment that would exempt people involved in that kind of forced-family splitting of assets from an increase in taxes? Has that matter been reconsidered, and can we expect an amendment that will remove that negative part of the Bill?

Mr. Chairman, I will repeat an answer that I gave this morning and on a previous day when we considered that question. I have to remind the Hon. Member that the law with respect to what a judge may do, as it pertains to property rights between spouses at termination of marriage, lies explicitly within the jurisdiction of the Provinces. The Hon. Member is obviously interested in the question because he has quoted statistics on marriage breakup. I suggest that he should address himself to the provincial jurisdiction in his efforts to obtain more humane treatment of people faced with this situation.
Income Tax
Life insurance, annuities, etc., is only one area that is affected by a court looking at a household. A consideration of the whole issue of matrimonial relations and how they are governed upon termination, has presumably to be done in a coordinated way so that it addresses not only life insurance but such things as real estate, family car, etc.
While the Hon. Member's interest is legitimate, I think it is directed to the wrong jurisdiction.

Mr. Chairman, I am not talking about the federal Government taking over provincial jurisdiction but about a federal tax law. I would point out to the Minister that people in the middle of a divorce will have to surrender assets, to use his own term, and will thus be liable for extra taxes.
If we proceed without the amendment which I suggest, then people in the midst of the most difficult time of their lives will be forced to incur an additional tax liability that they cannot afford. I am simply asking whether the Minister will bring forward an amendment in relation to the kinds of assets we are discussing that fall under federal jurisdiction so that the tax liabilities of the parties will not be increased. People do not want to surrender the assets but simply to split them. The technical part of the Bill requires them to surrender before the split, however, and this involves a tax liability which they do not need, do not want and which I do not think is humane. Would the Minister consider an amendment along the lines I have suggested?

Mr. Chairman, once again, the issue of how assets are dealt with by a court-whether they should be split, apportioned to one or the other, whether to set off one asset againt another, falls strictly within the provincial jurisdiction. In designing the rules for settlement, I think they have to take into account not only this law which deals with insurance but the law as it pertains to real property and other assets.
To be consistent, the question should be put to the Government that sets the rules about what happens upon dissolution of marriage.
Mr. Chairman, "consistency" is the operative word. Earlier we were talking about fairness. Does the Minister think it is fair to leave the law the way it is now?
Yes.

Another issue that 1 brought out was that of giving people the flexibility to change companies. We have regional insurance companies in Canada, but not all companies operate in all regions, yet we have a very mobile population. If this law passes in the way it is written, and I move, for example, from one region of Canada to another and I wish to change my insurance company, I will be required to surrender my first policy, pay tax on the accrued income, and have less money to invest in the subsequent policy. I will be at a disadvantage as compared to those people who do not move and choose to stay with the same company. Will the Minister consider this matter once again and consider allowing me to change insurance companies without having to pay tax?

March 10, 1983
Income Tax

The Hon. Member's concern is laudable. It is interesting to note that not a single insurance company in Canada, nor any consumer group, thought that the matter should be the subject of representation; there has been none. It reflects the reality of the improvement of the way in which not only the insurance business but financial services are offered across the country. There may be regional offices, but companies have the ability, inexpensively and quickly, to deal with Canadians moving from one coast to the other.

Earlier today I asked the Minister and his officials if they could use the lunch hour to enable them to indicate to us how much money historically had been accumulated through annuities and life insurance and thus was available as a pool of capital to lend out to business and industry to modernize and make our country more efficient and effective. Does the Minister have those figures at this point?

Mr. Chairman, I took advantage of the hour between one and two o'clock, in addition to answering telephone calls, signing letters, receiving other representations by officials and having lunch, to spend some time on the question raised by the Hon. Member. After reflection, I would again ask him to consider the area in which he is now inviting the Committee to enter. It is an area of capital markets and capital market formations, and it would be better addressed in another forum. I suggested this morning, for example, that when the Minister of Finance was before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs later this week or next week there would be an opportunity to ask him and his officials questions in that regard.
Capital formation is not restricted to insurance or annuity policies. The subject matter before the Committee at this time is not restricted or confined to the Income Tax Act. There are many other pressures or economic forces which come to bear on the larger issue. The Minister of Finance periodically reports on long-term, larger financial and economic projections and performance. I would recommend that this question be put before another forum so that, as the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North recommended, we could spend our time more profitably on the material which is actually before us.

I find it incredible that we can be considering such an important piece of tax legislation without any information or data on what it will do to capital formation in the country. This industry has been a significant part of how we have put together pools of capital to enable us to build plants, develop mines and drill for oil and gas. If we are destroying or hurting that market in any significant way, it simply means that there will be fewer jobs in the future. I draw to the attention of the New Democratic Party that without the formation of capital we cannot be productive and efficient and there will be no jobs. This is part of what has gone wrong in the country.
I remember standing in the House in October, 1980 and saying that if Members supported the National Energy Program, we would drive significant billions of dollars of capital out of the country and that if we did that, we would also drive out jobs and tax revenue. I stand here some two and a half years later, and all of that has come to pass. Capital was driven out of the country and jobs disappeared; we have 1.6 million unemployed. I am afraid that these few Clauses in the tax Bill may have similar implications in the future.
Also I am very disturbed that the Minister of Finance clearly indicated to the House that they have not done their homework, that they do not have data a projection or a guess about the degree to which capital markets will be hurt by this particular piece of legislation. This hurts job creation, this hurts the productivity of the nation, and it increases deficits. I think this matter is critically important, and I hope the Government will reconsider its position.
I would like to ask the Minister a few more questions. What happens if I have a life insurance policy which matures on my sixty-fifth birthday and I want to change it into an annuity to last through my retirement? Do I have to pay tax at that point?
The only exception to that case would be the one I indicated to the House in the case of disability, which obviously is not the case raised by the Hon. Member.

My question was: do I have to pay tax at that point? If my policy matures at age 65 and I want to change it at that point into an annuity, have I surrendered it at that stage and am I therefore eligible for tax before I move it into an annuity?
Yes, Mr. Chairman.
What happens if I die one day before that comes about? Do I have any tax liability at that point?
I assume not. If death occurs before the surrender is applied for or committed, the Hon. Member's estate merely receives the benefits from the policy without tax.
Is there a sense of fairness or a sense of justice in the fact that I can save a large tax bill by dying one day sooner?

I do not think the Hon. Member would be concerned at that point about whether or not he has saved anything. Probably in the back of his mind was his concern for his estate, his business partners and his family, which obviously was the reason he took out the policy in the first place. The benefits from the policy would be available to the estate in that case, and it would be a very commendable action on his part.

Why would the Government not just let me roll it into an annuity and, as I took it out on a monthly or yearly basis, let me pay the tax at the point at which I wanted to use the money I had saved all my life? Why could the Government not let me do it that way? Why does it have to
March 10, 1983

take some money before I can invest it in an annuity thus reducing the size of my annuity and my monthly payments for the rest of my life? The Government is really borrowing or taking my money before I have a chance to use it. Why could the Minister not consider an amendment of that kind?

In the Hon. Member's example he has received income. The principle of the Income Tax Act is to tax income. The Government uses the resources it gains through the taxation of income to meet some of its bills, presumably offering some of the services of the federal Government to the Hon. Member or to people associated with him. That is one of the major ways in which the Government of Canada finances public services.

Mr. Chairman, can the Minister see that if I have my assets in the form of grain in the granary which is there for my retirement, I will not be taxed on that unless I sell it? If I happen to live in a city and have been a salaried worker all my life, my life insurance policy is like the granary, but, all of a sudden, the day I turn 65, I will be taxed on the whole thing. Yet the other chap who has his money in a different form of asset, such as grain, will only be taxed when he delivers the grain to the station and sells it. Why do we have this kind of inequitable principle? A great many Canadians live on salary all their life. They do not have a whole lot of money. They would like to keep whatever they have been able to acquire to see them through their retirement years. Why is the Government stepping in and telling me that I am taking this into income when I am not? All I am trying to do is to invest it on a long term so it pays back a little every month rather than all at once. That is what I really want to do with it. Why will the tax man not allow me to do that?

Mr. Chairman, I would have to repeat my last answer. One of the major tax areas available to the Government is income tax. We do not have a grain tax or a grain collection system. Obviously, as the Hon. Member indicates, not everybody is into grain. We have an income tax system. It is a universal system. It is one where assets can be assessed on the basis of income easily identifiable in connection with financial institutions. It is a much more convenient way of assessing a plan against resources to be transferred into resources of the Government in order to finance Government services. We are being consistent, whether it is income which the Hon. Member earns through wages, through his occupation or through the sale of assets. The build-up in the life insurance policy that accrues over and above the cost of protection is viewed as income, and when received by people it is taxable under the Income Tax Act.

Mr. Chairman, earlier this day we talked about those Canadians who have a pension plan or an RRSP. If I were a small-businessman and I wanted to put something away for my retirement, I could put money in an RRSP, which is before-tax money. In other words, the taxpayer is making a partial contribution to my retirement by letting me defer tax
Income Tax
on that amount until retirement. What is the maximum amount of that deferral?
Mr. Chairman, if I understood the Hon. Member's question, for the RRSP it is $5,500 and for the RPP it is $3,500.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I advise the Hon. Member for Calgary West that his time on this point has expired.

Mr. Chairman, before my time expired last time, I was discussing with the Minister deferral of income. The Minister seems to indicate, in the way the Government is approaching these Sections, that people buy annuities, put money into guaranteed investment certificates, guaranteed investments, insurance policies that are single-premium pay insurance policies or accumulating funds only if they want to avoid income tax. The Minister knows that taxation is only one of the things that motivates people. Indeed, the Minister said that himself.
The Minister indicated earlier that there was a fair tax impact on the Government when the tax is not paid, it is deferred, taxes deferred are to some extent avoided. What studies does the Minister have in his Department with respect to what changing attitudes Canadians will have toward longterm savings as a result of the imposition of taxes on an accrual basis? What changing forms of investment are likely to take place? Does he not foresee that Canadians will, generally speaking, invest their money for shorter and shorter periods of time? On that basis, they will receive their income within the year and, therefore, have the income with which to pay the tax. Does he not foresee that indeed we will have shorter investment certificates-one year, no more than that. That is the kind of thing that is likely to develop? Will the Minister tell us what studies are available on how that will affect the long-term capital market?

Mr. Chairman, we know that Canadians are saving and probably investing at rates unparalleled in the history of Canada. Obviously there is room for debate as to whether investments should be locked up for 20 years, whether, as the Hon. Member for Mississauga South says, a move toward shorter investment is good or bad, or whether a move toward shorter investment permits people flexibility in being able to direct funds toward new opportunities in a fast paced technological world. It is almost impossible to guess or to generalize whether one is better than the other. I suppose a mixture is what will occur. Some people will go for short investments for their particular reasons while others will look for long-term investment for their particular reasons. That really is the choice of the individual. Surely, the Government should not be conducting in depth psychological analyses to try to mind-bend people as to what is the best investment for them.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister has already admitted that there has been a tremendous drop in the sale of deferred annuities. I suggest to the Minister that deferred

March 10, 1983
Income Tax
annuities as sold in Canada by Canadian life insurance companies to Canadians is a dead issue. No longer will they be sold. Nobody will buy them because they become taxable on an accrual basis. The only way an annuity earns is by accruing income and adding income to capital and capitalizing it, and so on. It is quite true you pay the tax on the income portion accumulated in the annuity as you draw out the money in the normal course. But now the system is that you pay the tax every three years at least, and there would be no way a person could invest in that type of certificate.
I suggest also to the Minister that cumulative GICs with trust companies are no longer a viable investment unit unless the cumulative period was less than three years.
I suggest to the Minister that single-pay premium life insurance policies that might, for one reason or another, be purchased by someone who had a block of cash and wants to protect an interest for a long period of time is no longer a viable method of protection because the single-pay policy causes the owner of the policy to be subject to tax every year or every three years on the imputed earnings behind the policy without receipt of income with which to pay the tax. I suggest to him that that form of long-term investment has been forced out. In other words, while these methods of investment may have been available as tax deferrals, at least the Government was getting taxes from the people who held these investments as the interest or other amount was paid out on the investments. Now that the Government has become so greedy as to collect its taxes on an annual accrual basis, it has, in effect, squeezed the neck of the golden goose so hard that there is no life in the goose at all. For all practical purposes it has wiped out accumulating GICs, accumulating bonds, accumulating deferred annuities and single-pay and accumulating investment type insurance policies. It has wiped out that source of investment opportunity for Canadians in Canada.
The Minister will know that we have pointed out that if Canadians want to invest in those type of instruments, there is no problem. They can go offshore to the United States or Great Britain. They can do this with a type of trust agreement, money fund or any number of ways. They are only prevented from doing it in Canada.
What studies has the Government done to determine what it really expects to accomplish with these Clause? What additional revenue does it really expect to receive? Having squeezed off the revenue source, is it not likely that the Government will receive no revenue? All it has done is to drive capital out of the country. Will the Minister tell us what revenue source the Government hopes to have as a result of these changes, bearing in mind that it has squeezed the neck of the golden goose so that there is no possibility of its even breathing, let alone laying eggs?

I believe that the Hon. Member's analysis is too narrow. His question is not as broadly focused as that of his colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West, who pointed out that one of the objectives of the tax policy certainly is a legitimate concern for job creation.
While the Hon. Member for Mississauga South may have a hang-up about interest-bearing securities and giving a preference to that kind of long-term investment, I would invite him to consider the same question that his colleague from Calgary West asked us to consider. Is that good for the mix that we would want in the economy, those investments in which we are trying to interest people who have funds available? Is a longterm debt security instrument, which has a preference over other types of investment opportunities such as shares and stocks necessarily the best thing that we should do at this time in the country? Is it the best thing to do when investment is down, production is down and the interest of small businessmen is at a low point? For example, they are not able to draw the same kind of investor interest in share or stock support for their projects.

I am glad that the Minister now realizes that what we are really talking about is jobs. We are really talking about the growth of the country and investment in the country.
What we are concerned about is the way these Clauses in particular and this Bill drive out long-term capital to other countries. The people who want to invest in this way are not prevented from doing so. They will not pay tax on their accumulating income. They will go somewhere else and do so without any problem.
Incidentally, the Minister said earlier that they would have to pay high-priced lawyers. Let me advise the Minister that the new round of accumulating money funds for investment offshore will now be sold in units of $1,000. They are not large units so that the ordinary Canadian will be able to buy them offshore in competition with Canada Savings Bonds and not have to worry about paying tax on the accumulating money as he will be required to do under this Bill.
Again, in terms of real revenue, what does the Minister really believe he will get by virtue of these Clauses? Does he think, for example, that by passing this kind of punitive measure he will somehow persuade Canadians who want to invest in instruments that are banned by this punitive measure to invest in something else in the country? Does he not think, though, that they will take their money somewhere else in the world where they can invest it as they please? What kind of revenue does the Minister hope to receive in the future by a tax on these kinds of investment vehicles?

Mr. Chairman, as I indicated earlier, the objective is to eliminate the drain which is a result of the deferral that otherwise would be available in these instruments, which is estimated to be some $75 million because of the high interest rates in the last two years. That is revenue that is not available to the Government in order to meet its obligations.
I point out as well that the Bill lowers the top marginal rate, which is a policy decision by the Government to induce those in the higher income brackets to be able to use the difference between the former rate and the lower rate for investment purposes. What this Clause does specifically is to take away the privileged or preferred spot that annuities held over such
March 10, 1983

other instruments in the economy which are the vehicles for the direct creation of jobs. I am talking about stock and bond opportunities for investment.
The Financial Post article which I drew to the Hon. Member's attention calls the buyers of this annuity instrument sophisticated, well-healed investors, perhaps a little wary of the stock market, who can afford to tie up income for a long time in order to avoid paying tax on it at current high marginal rates. We are trying to provide some direction through the marginal rate reduction, which I have discussed, and through increases in the small business limits to show that there is a need for investment in other areas. Certainly, the Government ought not to continue to provide such a nonproductive preference to non-job generating areas of return to investors.

It is unfortunate that we have a Minister of State for Finance who does not realize that a cumulative bond such as a Canada Savings Bond is precisely the same debt instrument as a bond that does not accumulate. The only difference between a cumulative certificate and an annual or semi-annual pay certificate is the date on which the payor is required to pay interest out to the payee. The money that goes into these certificates is precisely the same money that goes into any other certificate. Through these Clauses, the Minister is forcing those people who wish to have an accumulating type of investment, either a GIC, Canada Savings Bond or insurance policy or annuity, to go to some other country with their money where they will be treated honestly and fairly as they were by Governments in the past in this country.
We are talking about investment money being driven out of Canada because that money is invested where investors wish to place it. It is the absolute and supreme arrogance of the Minister and the Government for them to suggest that their tax laws can force investors to invest in modes in which they do not want to invest. Do they not realize that the 49th parallel is a pretty imaginary line and that investors can take their funds and invest them wherever they want in this big, wide world, and in the kinds of investment instruments that they want? They are not forced by the Minister or by the Income Tax Act in Canada to do something that they do not want to do. Therefore, we are really discussing jobs and investment, the creation of new opportunity, which the Government wants to drive out of the country.
Blindly, the Minister has decided that this is the way he should go. The philosophy was developed from the top floor of the Place Bell tower by people who have no understanding of the way the world works. They are hidebound in this city of Ottawa. Their vision of Canada is limited on the south by the airport and on the north by the Ottawa River. That is their vision. They do not know what is happening or where they are going.
I want to say that we will not carry on with these Sections much longer. As far as I am concerned, I will suggest that we vote on these Sections right now.
Income Tax
Eight minutes.
Here they are. They are all going to roar in now. The ducks are coming in, guys.
Powerful man.

speakerposition: Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
speechtext: Back in power.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: He's better than our Whip.
However, my colleague, the Hon. Member for Calgary West, says that he wants to speak for a while.
It is nice to have an audience for a change.
We will be here until six. We will be here today and tomorrow and Monday and Tuesday. Do not worry. We might as well pass it now. We will be here. No, no, the numbers game, we will not fail on that.

Just before my allotted time expired, I was asking the Minister how much money a small-businessman could shelter for retirement purposes, and the Minister said, $5,500 or $3,500. How much money can a Cabinet Minister shelter in his pension plan?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, all Members of Parliament, of course, follow the same sheltering rules as all Canadians follow. I understand that in after-tax dollars, we contribute more. However, we as a group are paying twice on those funds because we are taxed when we take them out again, too. Therefore, we pay for a good portion of our pension plans with after-tax dollars, and we pay again.

I was hoping I would hear the response that it is the same for all Canadians. I would bring to the Minister's attention the case involving corporate executives. Is it not true that an executive, himself, can put money in, but then the company can put in an almost unlimited amount to provide a pension of $60,000 a year, inflated, and that that money which the company puts in is not taken into income and is not taxed?

Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member has raised interesting subjects. However, again, with 150 clauses before us, I think we should really try to deal with items which are before us. I understand that it is not germane to the Act before the House.

The Minister stands and speaks of fairness time after time. I simply want information as to whether the system is fair. It is our conviction that life insurance and life insurance annuities are really the poor man's vehicle in preparation for retirement. They are in somewhat the same category as the family home. If one considers the assets of an average Canadian preparing for retirement, one finds that there may or may not be a pension plan. There is usually a family home involved, and there is quite often a life insurance policy or some kind of annuity which is bought in later life.
We on this side are suggesting that by becoming involved in the notion of accrual as it affects these Clauses, an additional

March 10, 1983
Income Tax
tax is really being placed on average Canadians. Those who are rich enough to afford gold, silver or stamps, or who have a granary full of grain, do not have to pay on the basis of accrual. They pay only at the moment they begin to use incomes. In this tax Bill there is a provision to tax when a court directs that assets of those involved in a divorce must be split. There is a provision by which tax accrues the minute people become age 65 and want to turn their savings into annuities. If this comes into the system, it will cause average Canadians to face an extra tax. That is the problem concerning this particular piece of legislation.
I want to deal with one last issue and lay it out on the table. Does the Department have an estimate of the cost to Canadian society of the additional paperwork which this change in law will require? Just think about it for a moment. Every policyholder in the country will have to be notified, and each letter will require a 32 to 35-cent stamp. Material setting out the calculations and so forth will be required, meaning additional cost to the industry to notify policy holders to their tax position. Does the Minister have an estimate of the cost to Canadian society?

Mr. Chairman, as the Hon. Member for Parry Sound-Muskoka indicated this morning, from his own investigation he found that only 5 per cent of life insurance policies, a very small amount, would be affected by the three year accrual route.
Further, we all know that insurance companies are leaders in terms of information management, of taking advantage of the new technological gains to assist them in very economic handling of all types of information recording, including the small 5 per cent of their policies which would be subject to the rules in the Bill before us. The information of the Hon. Member concerns the profile of persons taking advantage of annuities. His description of annuities as being the poor man's vehicle certainly does not coincide with that of the impartial writers and analysts of the situation. I would again refer the Hon. Member to The Financial Post of July 4, 1981. It states:
Annuity brokers say most contracts are for more than $10,000. Many exceed $100,000 and, occasionally, million-dollar contracts are sold.
I would be interested in the Hon. Member's definition of a poor man.

I think the words I used were "average Canadian". Certainly, at the age of 65, having a $10,000 cash surrender value which one desires to turn into an annuity is not a rich man's game. If one reads the article carefully, one finds that, yes, there are some policies sold for $1 million, and tax laws can be written specifically for those kinds of cases. However, in reality, I would certainly not describe the number of people who will get caught in this as being wealthy.
The question which I asked was whether the Department has an estimate of the increased cost through the paper
burden. The Minister indicates that in his opinion this cost is going to be slight, but there does not seem to be any data available.
Has the Department considered the increased cost to every partnership in the country which will have to re-write partnership agreements as their business expands, as dollar volumes change and the previous insurance policy that they had becomes inadequate and therefore has to be redone? Mr. Chairman, I have a few comments to make about automobile standby charges, and I have a couple of questions for the Minister. The auto standby charge is a tax levied on the personal use of company cars. The Bill proposes that the tax be raised from 1 per cent per month of the value of the car to 2 per cent per month, and in the case of lease cars the tax would be two-thirds of the lease cost. The 2.5 per cent figure in the November 12 budget has been revised downward to satisfy the initial burst of opposition. In cases where personal use does not exceed 1,000 kilometres per month, 12,000 per year, the standby charge would be reduced proportionately. The impact on the individual taxpayer is that the change will effectively double the tax payable by persons using company automobiles. It can be expected that this will reduce the desirability of company cars dramatically.
The over-all impact is that industry reaction focuses on the effect of the change on the purchase and operation of company cars. The initial result will be reduced orders for company fleets and reduced inventories for leasing agencies. Further opposition centers on the process of implementation of the changes. Confusion surrounding the calculation of the taxable benefit, the timing of the changes coming into force and the effect of terminal charges serves to perpetuate the general uncertainty of this proposal.
The Progressive Conservative Party position is as follows: While the principle of taxing this benefit is not unacceptable, the rate of taxation and the method of calculation is suspect. The negative impact of the tax increase overshadows the benefits of increased revenues. It should be amended downward. The sections of the Act dealing with calculation of benefits should be clarified along with the regulations.
I am sure all Members have received complaints from the Commercial Travellers' Association of Canada. They have sent us detailed letters on the adverse effects of this change. They point out that clearly the standby charge, based on an

Personal use is at an absolute minimum.

This letter was sent to the Minister of Finance in January of this year. I hope the Minister will give an indication of changes he will be making to this automobile standby charge.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, we will check that for the Hon. Member. None of the four of us here have that information.

Let us assume it is 20 cents a kilometre, Mr. Chairman. If I were to use my car 10,000 kilometres a month on behalf of the Government, that would be $2,000 worth of tax-free income, some of which would have to go toward the cost of gasoline, maintenance and so on. Do you think I might be able to pay for my car in a relatively short period of time with tax-free dollars under that system?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, if it is strictly for business use or, as in his example, Government use, if it is not for the personal benefit of the taxpayer, that is fine. I would imagine equally that if the Hon. Member used a vehicle for that number of kilometres per month he would wear it out in a hurry.
March 10, 1983

Mr. Chairman, if it is true that I am using my personal car on behalf of my employer and taking mileage in, there is no tax on the portion of personal use, in other words, I can, by doing that, get my car paid for with tax-free dollars.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member has the principle under control, and I congratulate him. For business use it is tax-free. For personal use it is after-tax dollars. If a taxpayer buys his own car and he gets a portion of his own car paid for because of business use, that portion will be tax exempt. If, on the other hand, the employer supplies the car, and the employee uses the car a portion of the time for his own use, that portion will be added on as a taxable benefit to the taxpayer's income. The Hon. Member has the principle under control. If the vehicle is used for personal use, then it is taxed. If it is used for business use, then it is not taxed.

We are beginning to learn, Mr. Chairman. In Western Canada there are a number of one-man RCMP detachments in the small communities and rural areas. Those RCMP officers must be on duty 24 hours a day. Generally, many of them are single. The RCMP squad car has a radio for contact purposes. If an RCMP constable uses the car to go down the road to a dance on Friday evening for pleasure, is that a taxable use of the Government of Canada automobile? Has that directive gone out to the RCMP?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would assume that is a personal use of the vehicle, and, therefore, is a taxable use. If the Hon. Member is making a representation to us, then we will bring it to the attention of the Solicitor General.

Mr. Chairman, does the Minister or his Parliamentary Secretary have certain knowledge that such a directive has gone out to the RCMP, that if they use the squad car to go to the corner grocery store they will be taxed on it? How do we decide whether it is business or not when a human being is on 24-hour call and the radio by which they are called is in the vehicle? The radio is in the vehicle. They are on call 24 hours a day. They also have to live, they have to go to the grocery store, they have to have entertainment, and yet they! have to have radio contact at the same time. How do they separate business from pleasure?

Mr. Chairman, on this side we have confidence that the RCMP act in all they do honestly, accurately, and efficiently. Whatever directives they receive from their superiors are ones they follow honestly.
However, the Hon. Member does hit upon a policy that is adopted by some police forces in some cities across the country. They request police officers to take police vehicles to their homes when they are not "on duty". The point is that the presence of the police vehicle with its markings acts throughout the community as a deterrent and a security source. Therefore, I would think that on looking at what is the definition of the use of the vehicle at that time, it would be concluded in some circumstances that the vehicle was being used at all times, whether at home or in the business community, for purposes of security and, therefore, is business.
Income Tax

Mr. Chairman, if you accept that principle, then suppose I have a company and a number of company vehicles. I put my logo on the car door. Now I can encourage my employees to drive to and from work. That will be considered business rather than personal use simply because I want my logo advertised throughout the community. Is that a ruling from the Minister with which people can live?
I do not think the two examples are at all parallel, Mr. Chairman.
Why not?

I cannot recall precisely the Minister's words, but the particular form of the police vehicle, the colour, the presence of an aerial perhaps, acts as a deterrent throughout the community. Certainly it is good for my business if my logo is seen throughout the community. In fact, many businesses spend lots of money on advertising by painting their logos on car doors. Why can I not argue with Revenue Canada that it is good for my business for my employees to take those vehicles and drive them throughout the community on all occasions, for example, drive to the store, drive to a social event, and so on? Why would it not be all business if my car had a logo on it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the Hon. Member could argue his case. Go ahead. I would suggest that if he looks at the debate on this whole issue, he would find that we followed his line of thought with automobile salesmen who were successful in telling us that by driving their product home, they were, in fact, advertising. It is for that reason that automobile salesmen pay a lower standby charge than other salesmen do for personal use. They do, indeed, follow the practice described by the Hon. Member. There was considerable debate on this, and other groups were not able to present their cases successfully. I would suggest, on a case by case basis, that the Hon. Member might be successful in demonstrating that such advertising or such behaviour would not constitute personal use but would constitute business use. Perhaps if he can think of examples, he could pursue them.

Mr. Chairman, can we pursue a couple more? Let us assume I own a fair sized farm which I have incorporated. The vehicles belong to the corporation, which is in reality my farm. If I use the automobile on the farm, the pickup truck or the four-wheel drive to go 15 miles to the local town or village to buy supplies and then drive back to the farm, is that business use or personal use?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I think the Hon. Member is in an area of interpretation where it might be useful to raise this issue with Revenue Canada instead of in Committee of the Whole.

I think it is our responsibility as Parliamentarians to provide sufficient definitions to legislation so that Canadians can understand their tax liabilities as a consequence of the definitions. Does the Minister not believe that it is the

March 10, 1983
Income Tax
responsibility of Parliament to define the terms? We are trying to separate business from personal use. We either do it in a clear-cut from in legislation or we turn it over to the bureaucrats or the courts. If we are to tax people on the difference between business and personal use, it is our job as Parliamentarians to try to define it. Is it not our job to define those terms?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: I would remind the Hon. Member that we are not operating in a vacuum with this measure. We have had this measure since 1971. The questions he raises about people driving from their farm to the city or people who drive with their logos on the side of their cars have all been asked. There is a body of experience on those questions now. The questions that he is raising are hypothetical. He would probably be well advised to refer to that body of experience and to the debates in places such as the parliamentary committee in order to familiarize himself with the background on this. We are not dealing with a new measure. We are dealing with hypothetical views on a body of experience.

The Minister indicated earlier in this discussion that there was a new part ot this provision, which is the one dealing with operating costs. Maintenance is part of operating costs. Is maintenance to be valued at market value or at some other value which I choose to put on it?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, whatever the employer uses as an expense would be the value that would be put on for the employee.

If I live in a high-class area where we use a commercial garage to fix something, and I drive the vehicle 1,000 kilometers a month so that I am eligible for 24 per cent, I will pay more in taxes than someone who works for a compay which has a mechanic who fixes the automobile and there is no direct charge to that automobile. Will we have this type of difference, or would I have to keep track of the commercial value of every automobile that I fix in the fleet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, it is expenses. Bear in mind that we are talking about expenses for personal use. If it was someone's personal car, the same principle would hold true. In higher cost areas one would pay higher cost after tax, and in lower cost areas one pays lower cost after tax. It is a simple principle of paying tax on personal use.

Perhaps I was not very clear. Suppose that I work for a small company and I cannot afford a mechanic. I drive the company's automobile 1,000 kilometres a month. Therefore I have to take into income 24 per cent of the maintenance costs of that particular automobile. Suppose my friend seated next to me works for a large company with many automobiles and that company has its own garage and staff. It does not charge for maintenance or repairs, it simply absorbs it. Therefore, working for a small company, I pay more tax than my friend. Is that the kind of tax system we are putting in place?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to be able to clear this up. I am sorry I did not do so in the last round. The cost of the mechanics would be prorated over the cars because those are the expenses that the employer is writing off for the fleet.
Could the Hon. Member point out to me where, in the legislation, I am allowed to average repair costs over a fleet?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, that is a practice for Revenue Canada to determine.

Mr. Chairman, we have been having a long but interesting discussion dealing with the various kinds of expenses which employers can charge off because the cars are used for business purposes. There are also provisions in the Income Tax Act to allow self-employed people such as salesmen, doctors and lawyers to charge off the expenses of their cars for gas, oil, maintenance, insurance and, 1 presume, depreciation to the extent that those cars are used for business.
Is the Government giving consideration to the problems of thousands of Canadians who are not self-employed doctors, lawyers or salesmen but must use their cars because of the vast distances they must drive to work? There are Canadians who have no choice but to drive up to 50 miles to work because in most cities the public transit system does not get them to work on time. Is the Government giving any consideration to those hundreds of thousands of people who are spending large amounts of money each year to go to and from work? They do not have the same ability, because our tax laws do not permit it, to charge off part of the expenses of their automobile transportation. It is a necessary expense for them in order to keep their job and earn their money.

Mr. Chairman, there is a general employment deduction or expense allowance. Of course, the result of the increase in the tax from 1 per cent to 2 per cent to those people, such as in the example of doctors and lawyers used by the Hon. Member, whose occupation is in fact their business, brings in more revenue to assist in the provision of services to people generally.
Finally, I do not take such a pessimistic view of the role of public transit as that which the Hon. Member seems to have adopted in his preamble. I think that the opportunities for the improvement and enhancement of public transit in Canada are great. For example, the federal Government has supported both the research and technology for the improvement of public transit facilities. For example, we have supported the trial system in the City of Vancouver which will indirectly result in the mass production of these types of systems that will be available to Canadians in larger numbers and large urban areas in particular.

I do not think the Minister understood my point. If he were to visit the Oakville automobile plant and talk to the people who work there and who come there by car, he would find that many of them live as far as 40 miles from Oakville. If he were to go to Thunder Bay and talk to the
March 10, 1983

people who work in the grain elevators, he would find that there are people who live 20 miles, 30 miles, and 40 miles from the grain elevator. If he visited the people who work in the rolling mills in Selkirk, Manitoba, he would find that they drive from Gimli or other places that are miles away.
I am asking if the Government is giving consideration to applying the same principle to people who work for a company and have to drive long distances to get there. Is the Government giving the same kind of consideration to tax concessions to workers as are now given to self-employed people or those who work in the categories we have been discussing, such as those who use their own cars?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member has hit upon a very important point. His point, in effect, is what the current provisions are doing. The Hon. Member has described, for example, the great distances that people drive to work. I would remind him that under this legislation, personal use of a vehicle and expenses for that kind of driving, along with some of the other employment expenses involved, are covered under the employment deduction which the Minister mentioned. I would also remind the Hon. Member that the self-employed person, the professional or the salesman who only uses a vehicle to go from the place of work to the home, is using that car for personal use, and it is precisely for that reason that we are hearing some of the complaints from the Conservative benches.

Mr. Chairman, I am sorry, but I did not understand the explanation that the Parliamentary Secretary gave me. Is he saying that it is considered personal use for a person to drive a car from home to work? That is precisely the point I am trying to make. One can hardly call using one's car to get to work personal driving when it is the only way one can get to work. If one did not get to work, one would not earn a living and one would not be in a position to pay income tax or anything else.
It's an employment expense.

It's an expense of employment, Mr. Chairman. What I am saying to the Government is that I know nothing has been done until now. In my view, people who must use their cars to get to work, who must drive substantial distances, should be treated no differently from the salesman who travels from Winnipeg to Regina, stopping on the way to make calls and, hopefully, to make sales. He is using the car to make sales, to earn his commission, to earn a living, in the same way a person driving his car from Winnipeg to Selkirk to work in the rolling mills is using his car to earn a living. Therefore, what I am saying is that 1 would like the Government to give serious consideration to making some provisions to benefit these people in the same spirit as is now evident with regard to self-employed people or others who work in the way we have been discussing this afternoon. They should be given the same kind of consideration and same ability to deduct expenses incurred travelling to and from work, as self-
Income Tax
employed and other people have been afforded for a number of years in this country.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
It is an interesting perspective to the problem which the Hon. Member has put forth. I would simply urge him to consider equally the fact that the employment expense deduction is designed to do exactly what he is describing. How, for example, would he calculate the benefit of someone travelling by public transit versus someone travelling by automobile? Should we assume that people travelling by public transit should simply be allowed a great big deduction to make them equal to the people who travel by automobile? I think that if he begins to draw those parallels, he should take them right through all the logical steps instead of stopping where he did. I would urge him to realize that the Government proposed the employment expense deduction precisely to avoid that kind of detailed calculation involving streetcar or automobile expenses.
The Hon. Member is quite correct in the way that he has described these employment related expenses. However, I would suggest to him that these are already covered under the deductions which every taxpayer is entitled to enjoy at this point. Concerning automobile expenses, we are trying to ensure that automobile usage by professionals, self-employed people and salesmen is treated in the same way as usage by the employees he has described, and that there is no special advantage for them in the way that he fears.

I raise problems of a different category of workers, the problems which have been brought to the attention of the Government on a number of occasions in recent years by the building trade unions. Construction workers very frequently must travel very long distances from home in order to get to work. Until about a year ago, the economy in Alberta and Saskatchewan was very active. There were a large number of big, ongoing construction projects. Construction in Manitoba was slow. A large number of construction and skilled workers from Manitoba went to Alberta and Saskatchewan. They have spoken to me, to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of National Revenue of their problems. As they explained in their annual submissions, they travel 500 to 600 miles away from home. They leave their families at home. Family expenses continue, as always. They work on construction sites.
A recent example was that of a Winnipeg worker on a power project in Saskatchewan. He had to travel from home to the power project and stay there for two or three weeks. Because he wanted to see his family and, in fact, keep his family together, he would make the 500 or 600 mile journey from the construction site to his home and then go back at the end of the weekend. Therefore, he made a round trip of 1,000 or 1,200 miles. I wonder why that worker should not be able to deduct the expenses involved in that kind of trip which was necessary, not only for his job but also if he was to keep his family together. I wonder why he should not be able to deduct part of his automobile expenses in the same manner as self employed people.

March 10, 1983
Income Tax

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the Hon. Member has waxed eloquent on many worker-related topics. I would suggest that he might want to raise some of these questions when we consider some of the other provisions in the Act. For example, for workers who are at temporary work sites, there are now some special considerations as to the benefits they receive there, i would hope that he would examine those and take into consideration the fact that we have relieved those people of some of the previous tax burdens that they faced.
I would hope, as well, that he would consider the increases which we have brought about this year, for instance, in Child Tax Credits, or the $200 spousal transfers and the decreases in the general tax rates which we have introduced. If the Hon. Member wants to speak in general terms of workers and the way they are affected by the Act, he should consider some of those questions as well. Above all, I think he wants to return to his main point which concerns the question of equity.
In his case, he has raised his concern about salesmen, doctors or other professionals and self employed people who somehow derive a benefit for which every one else pays but which is denied to everyone else. I want to set the record straight. I want him to know that what we are trying to do is the very thing that he is urging us to do. We are trying to create equity involving employee benefits. We are trying to ensure that workers who do not enjoy certain benefits can see that the benefit is, nevertheless, deserved. In other words, workers will see that if they are not allowed a car write-off themselves, their company benefits from the activity of a salesman who goes out in his car and brings in new orders. They will see equally that when the salesman uses his car for personal use, he does so in the same way as they do. He pays for that car in after-tax dollars. He makes use of the car in after-tax dollars.
That is the intention of this Clause. We are not trying to set up yet one more benefit for another group. We are in fact trying to remove unjustified benefits and we are trying define more clearly the benefit that is business-related and productive, which keeps other people employed. When a benefit does that, we are prepared to say that it should be a tax-exempt activity, that the individual who takes his car and goes out and gets orders or generates new sales for a business is doing something on behalf of that business which he should not have to pay tax on. It does not matter whether the individual is doing that in his own car and getting mileage payments, or whether he is using the company car and getting it tax-free. As long as it is business-related, the individual should not be paying tax on the use of that vehicle. If it is personal, if it is something that aids the individual's personal life, then he should be enjoying that benefit with after-tax dollars. That is all we are asking here.
We have heard from the Conservative benches that the application of this rule is harsh, but in fact it is not. All we are saying is that the salesman who drives the car on a holiday to Florida or a lawyer who drives his car back and forth to the
office every day, and that is the extent of it, or some selfemployed man who enjoys the car 50 per cent of the time for his own use and 50 per cent for business, should pay tax because everyone else in the same circumstances is using a car purchased with after-tax dollars.
The Hon. Member has asked about individuals driving to and from work. I have tried to clear up with him the principle that such driving is a general employment expense and that we have given all taxpayers a general employment deduction. It is much simpler for us to use one deduction of that nature than it is to create a whole bunch of categories, so much for shoes, so much for bus fare, so much for cars, so much for uniforms and so on. That is not a reasonable kind of categorization of employment expenses. Instead of getting into that sort of very detailed consideration, we have given a general flat deduction.
If the Hon. Member would like to raise that deduction and discuss with us the size of the deduction, we would be happy to hear his comments. We would like to know if he feels that that deduction is too low. Let us bear in mind that such a deduction would apply not only to the individual working on the assembly line but would also apply to the salesman driving a company car. It is the principal equity that we are concerned with here.
We want the Hon. Member to understand that we are not trying to single out and give a benefit to a salesman or to a worker or to someone who drives a short distance or a long distance. We are not trying to create special categories. What we are trying to do is to remove those special categories and get back to simple, basic principles, namely, if a vehicle or any other benefit is employment-related then it is tax-free because it is productive. It adds to the economy; it creates jobs; but if a vehicle or any other benefit is used for personal use then it should be paid for in after-tax dollars.
I would like to point out to the Hon. Member that that is all we are doing, asking for after-tax dollars for personal use of the vehicle. The salesman, the self-employed person, the professional, can avoid this problem altogether simply by not using the car for any kind of personal use. That seems to be a heresy for some people, but 1 find it quite a simple, direct proposition. If one feels that the car is too expensive, then one should not use it for personal use but only for business use. But if it is felt to be reasonable to pay a bit of tax for a bit of personal use, then there is a fairly inexpensive car. Treated fairly, every other taxpayer can look on that vehicle and see that it is paid for on an after-tax basis and that it is not a special perk for a special individual.
I hope the Hon. Member takes some of these principles to mind. He has waxed eloquent on the problems of people who live a long way away from their business, and who have to drive there. Equally, I would ask him to reflect on the complexities of bringing in all these special considerations for every worker. Should we ask that worker, for example, to keep mileage charts? Should we ask the worker to keep receipts for boots that he has to buy for his work? Should we ask the worker to keep receipts for uniforms? Instead of getting into that complexity, we have just suggested a flat deduction which
March 10, 1983

the individual can enjoy, whether he has an expense or not, and we think that is a fair and straightforward procedure and it applies to self-employed people and to workers, to professionals and to men and women on assembly lines.
I hope the Hon. Member will take that into account and try to give us his reaction about the more general category of the employment deduction, rather than to try to split that deduction into specific categories that would add incredible headaches and complexity to every working man and woman in this country. We have heard from people all over the country that the tax form is already too complicated. We have heard that it is difficult to understand the Income Tax Act, and I urge the Hon. Member to realize that the Income Tax Act would be made worse by the kind of proposal that he is making. I think we would hear very fruitfully from him about the size of the deduction, but I would urge him not to get into special categories beyond that deduction, because it would make the situation even worse.
Great filibuster speech!

Mr. Chairman, I think it would be very helpful in this type of discussion if we could perhaps get down to more specifics, and I would like to address my question to the Minister. I take it that the Minister is supplied with a Government car. Is that correct?

Mr. Chairman, the vehicle that I originally used was one that came to me when I was Minister of Public Works responsible for CMHC and the NCC. When I had the opportunity of changing Ministries and accepting responsibility for the Ministry of State for Finance, because it was the first time I had had the opportunity of changing portfolios and the second opportunity I had had of accepting a portfolio in this Government, it was new to me, but the system then provided that, with changes in those responsibilities, the vehicle that was assigned to the Minister in the original portfolio remained with that Minister in that portfolio. Unfortunately, that vehicle was on its last legs, and after letting me down on a number of occasions when I had to hail cabs or look for help from garages and the like, I had to look for yet another vehicle. That vehicle has only been of use and provided to me while on Departmental or Government business in the City of Ottawa. When I travel to my own constituency, and I do that each weekend, or on Government business in other Provinces, of course I would look for transportation-
