subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES. (B) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW. (C) REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF MONITORING OFFICER
THE ADMINISTRATION-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES. (B) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW. (C) REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF MONITORING OFFICER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the course of the last couple of days I have been directing a series of questions to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. MacEachen) about the Government's attitude toward the conflict of interest guidelines which appear to so clearly have been breached in the Alastair Gillespie Affair.
What is clear from the attitude of the Government to date is that the Government is not concerned about the whole issue of conflict of interest. It is concerned about the public relations aspect of the issue, whether or not the reputation of the Government has been injured by the way it has performed. It is not concerned about ensuring that there are comprehensive guidelines, which are tough, which are strict, which are enforced and which ensure the highest standards of probity on the part of Government officials.
On reading the guidelines any reasonable person would see that the guidelines have been breached. They have been breached with complicity of the Government. Mr. Gillespie was not alone in this affair. He had to do what he did with the co-operation of the Government. The Government's response has been to deny that lobbying is lobbying. It decided to reinvent and redefine the word in its own way to ensure that what Mr. Gillespie did in asking for the support and guidance of his former Deputy Minister, did not constitute lobbying in the opinion of the Government.
Secondly, the guidelines refer to undue influence or the appearance of undue influence. When Mr. Gillespie was able to get immediate access to his former Deputy Minister and able to get the rules changed for his particular proposal, the Government simply said that in its opinion this did not constitute undue influence on the part of Mr. Gillespie. What it has done is to render the guidelines absolutely meaningless. Any

March 10, 1983
Adjournment Debate
reasonable person examining the guidelines, if the guidelines were at all meaningful, would have concluded that the guidelines had been breached.
The second question Parliament must ask is, if the guidelines are breached, what teeth is there in them, what sanction is there and what ability is there to help people to account for breaches of the guidelines? Any Government with integrity would have required that Ministers who were responsible for breaches of guidelines must resign. If they were not prepared to go themselves, the Prime Minister had the obligation to fire them.
However, we find that the Prime Minister tells me, in answer to questions I put to him in the House, confirmed by the Deputy Prime Minister, that what they are toying with, in a review of the conflict of interest guidelines is a watering down. If the Gillespie affair was to happen again, they would not do anything to change the guidelines to ensure that proper conduct was to be followed by the Government. They would rewrite the guidelines to ensure that no one could claim that guidelines had been breached.
I said yesterday in the House that that sort of procedure was tantamount to the Liberal's discovering that a Liberal was caught trying to burn down the Parliament Buildings and the Government then legalized arson. It is very easy to ensure that the guidelines are never breached if the guidelines are rendered meaningless. If the Government were serious about putting an end to the concern that exist in this affair, it would have been candid with Parliament. Parliament would not have been misled in the first place. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Chretien) have conceded that Parliament was misled. When the Government tabled documents in the House, it would have made an effort to ensure that all relevant documents were tabled.
Following Question Period, the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley) tabled documents relating to the Cape Breton Development Corporation. He indicated when he spoke in the House that if one looked at the documents, he would find that in each case there was a note there with respect to particular minutes about documents which were not included in detail. When I ask him about it, he made it very clear that some of the documents had been laundered or deleted in his review of the files. Yet when you look at the material produced by the Minister, there are no notes indicating which documents have been deleted from the file. Again, the Government has not been candid with Parliament.
What should the Government be doing? First, Mr. Speaker, if the Government were serious about making the conflict of interest guidelines meaningful, it would strike a parliamentary committee, not have the in-house whitewash review, designed to water down the guidelines, contemplated by the Prime Minister. Instead, we should have a parliamentary committee charged with the responsibility of writing a meaningful set of guidelines and enforcement procedures.
I think one of the key elements of such a study would be a finding that it is time to have an officer of Parliament charged with the responsibility of investigating alleged breaches of the guidelines, and making a report to Parliament which could then be acted upon by a parliamentary committee. That is what is being done in the United States in many jurisdictions where they have ethics committees. In our case, that would be tantamount to having the Chief Electoral Commissioner given the responsibility of enforcing guidelines on ethics, not just during election campaigns, but also with regard to conflict of interest by officials and former officials. A report to Parliament could be made by this independent officer of Parliament and, if it appeared that the evidence warranted further study, a parliamentary committee could be called in.
It is essential that the Government act now, Mr. Speaker, to cut out the cancer which is growing here; the cancer of cover up and patronage which is rampant in this Government; the cancer of decline in public trust in the behaviour of public officials. It could do that by plugging Parliament back into the process, by striking that parliamentary committee and ensuring the sort of independent review of conflict of interest which I have suggested. Anything less than that can only damage the reputation of Parliament, and can only weaken the regard in which public life is held by ordinary Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. David Smith (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: THE ADMINISTRATION-CONFLICT OF INTEREST GUIDELINES. (B) REQUEST FOR COMMITTEE REVIEW. (C) REQUEST FOR APPOINTMENT OF MONITORING OFFICER
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Wellington-Duffer-in-Simcoe (Mr. Beatty) has been suggesting that the conflict of interest guidelines should be referred to a parliamentary committee for review, and further, that a parliamentary auditor be appointed to monitor and report to Parliament on the application of these guidelines. It is hard to believe the Hon. Member is serious. In view of the totally irresponsible and outrageous way in which this Member and his colleagues in both Opposition Parties have comported themselves on this issue in the House, I do not see any benefit at all in the Government referring this question to a committee. In fact, this would probably be the worst thing we could do to Parliament. It would reopen the vicious unfounded attacks on Hon. Ministers, unnecessarily ruin reputable careers, and further tarnish the image of the House of Commons in the minds of all Canadians.
The value of the present and any future guidelines rests with the integrity of Members of Parliament. It is indeed unfortunate that this fundamental principle has been put to such unfair tests in the last few weeks. I for one believe in the basic principles of democracy. One of these principles is the integrity and good faith of public officials. Without this trust our system cannot operate. This trust cannot be engendered by the creation of yet another bureaucratic watchdog. I would hope after the bitter debate of the last two weeks, Parliamentarians would now unite and reinforce the will of Parliament to deal with the major issues facing the country.
Perhaps the Hon. Member should reflect upon the proposal he has recently advanced to create another officer of Parliament. In a time of severe economic restraint, the Opposition is recommending the establishment of a new bureaucratic
March 10, 1983

organization. Not only would this be a waste of taxpayers' money, but it is also not at all related to the prime objective of this Government, to rebuild the economic well-being of our country. Surely the Opposition does not wish to dilute the impact of this Government's economic recovery program by spending more money to increase the Parliamentary bureaucracy.
In closing, Mr. Speaker, I would again ask that Members of the Opposition read the present conflict of interest guidelines. Now more than ever it is important that Members forget their partisan role, fully understand the guidelines, interpret them in a just and fair way, and start acting like Parliamentarians.

AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN CONTENT LEGISLATION BE ENACTED. (B) CANADA-JAPAN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to pursue this issue in relation to a question I put to the Minister of State for International Trade (Mr. Regan) on March 1, about the failure of the Canadian Government to negotiate for Canadian content in Japanese cars sold in this country.
A short time ago, General Motors and Toyota in California were able to come to an agreement whereby Toyota, in partnership with General Motors, would establish a plant there which would give jobs to about 12,000 Americans.
[ Translation]
There are many other examples of countries throughout the world where a national corporation has an agreement with a Japanese company. I am thinking about Peru, Brazil, Australia and France, all of which have negotiated an agreement with Japan to have a national content in the manufacture of Japanese vehicles. I believe that we could have the same type of agreement in Canada if our ministers negotiated more earnestly than they have done in the past.

I suggest that we should give the Minister more bargaining power. I think the Government should introduce for first reading in this House a Canadian content bill which would provide that 85 per cent of the content of Japanese cars in this country should be Canadian. In other words, if $1 million worth of Japanese cars were sold in Canada, $850,000 worth of the construction cost should be Canadian. This would create more jobs. I make this suggestion because I want to give the Minister some more clout. I do not suggest that we should pass the bill at all stages at this time, but just that it should be
Adjournment Debate
introduced for first reading. That would enable the Minister to go to Tokyo to meet his counterpart there and point out how worried we are about the situation.
At the moment, 25 per cent of our automobile market goes to Japanese cars. We recognize that they have some of the most efficient and beautiful cars in the world, and Canadians want to drive them, but we also want to make them in Canada. Our people want the jobs. They do not like the idea of buying a Japanese car, or any other foreign product, thus creating jobs elsewhere. More manufacturing in Canada would create more jobs and put the country back to work, making it more productive and wealthy.
When the Parliamentary Secretary responds I hope he will not reject my idea out of hand. I hope he will lend support to the proposition that we must be tough negotiators, no matter with whom we deal. I have heard many trade commissioners and others involved in foreign trade describe us as the "Boy Scouts" of international trade. In many ways we are really the pussycats of international trade and, Mr. Speaker, our claws are being pulled. It is time for us to be tough. We can learn from the Americans, from the French, the Germans and the Japanese how to drive a tough bargain. I do not think anyone respects a country that bows to a threat, and that is what we have been doing. We have been much too meek and mild.
We are the sixth largest consumer of cars in the world and the third largest consumer of Japanese cars, after the United States and West Germany. That gives us clout with the Japanese. We are their third largest market and they want to keep that market and expand it. We sell valuable raw resources to Japan that are fabricated over there, giving jobs to the Japanese. I commend the Japanese for their tough bargaining. In return, I am just asking the Japanese that we do the same thing. We can purchase their cars but we could construct at least 85 per cent of them in this country as well, so that we could give jobs to Canadian workers in the manufacturing of cars. It also seems that this would be an excellent idea for western Canada. The car plants could be located there, very close to Japan compared with Central and Eastern Canada, and many Japanese cars are purchased by western Canadians. I think it makes sense all around.
The Australians, Mexicans, Peruvians and Brazilians with smaller markets are purchasing fewer Japanese cars than we are. If they can negotiate a deal with the Japanese, I wonder why we cannot, since we have the third largest Japanese car market in the world. We are a much bigger country and should have a lot more clout. If they can do it, we can do it. If the Americans can do, we can do it. We are no worse off than the Americans. We are no less imaginative than the Americans. We are no worse bargainers or traders than the Americans. If they can have Japanese car plants in their country, we can have them as well. If we do not, the time will come, in ten or 15 years, when we will still be importing Japanese cars, but instead of importing them all from Japan, we will be importing

them from California, Ohio and other places in the United States. This would even compound the problem we have today.
I appeal to the Government to use a little foresight, be tough, use some imagination and insist that Japanese negotiators treat us as fairly as they treat the Australians, Mexicans, Americans, and many other people around the world. If they do that with us, I will be pleased because we will have Canadian jobs.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jean Lapierre (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: AUTOMOTIVE INDUSTRY-REQUEST THAT CANADIAN CONTENT LEGISLATION BE ENACTED. (B) CANADA-JAPAN NEGOTIATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to the Hon. Member, I would like to point out that, in my opinion, if the Government had such a simplistic approach to our exchanges with Japan, nearly 93,000 jobs would be threatened in Canada. If we looked strictly at the automobile market, there would obviously be cause for concern. However, I would ask the Hon. Member to look at this in perspective and to realize that Canada, contrary to other countries which envy its position, such as the United States, Europe, and so on, has a positive balance of trade with Japan, which is certainly not the case of some of its other commercial partners whose balance of trade is negative. Mr. Speaker, it is easy to say: Let us become protectionists and threaten to adopt protectionist measures to strengthen our negotiating position. However, we are well aware that 600,000 jobs in Canada are directly dependent on a healthy export market. We are also well aware that 30 per cent of our economy operates under the rules of the open market. In my opinion, we would be worse off if the open market were to be ruled by tariffs, which would reduce our exchanges with markets such as Japan. The Hon. Member was also over-simplifying when he said that we sold only raw materials to the Japanese. I would like to point out to him that in 1981, 34.6
per cent of Canadian products sold to Japan were food products and that 24.5 per cent were semi-processed and processed products. However, Mr. Speaker, because of his own bill, I understand of course the frustration which the Hon. Member feels towards Japanese car manufacturers. On the other hand, I would ask him to have confidence in the outcome of our negotiations this spring, where we shall once again be able to bring pressure to bear on our Japanese partners.
1 would also ask him not to jump to conclusions regarding the outcome of the automobile task force created by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Lumley). I believe that the Hon. Member is panicking while, considering his concern for the commercial relations of Canada, he should develop a global approach and realize that Canadians have an advantage over Americans and Europeans and should certainly not feel inferior. On the contrary, other countries have much to learn from us.
As for the California project mentioned by the Hon. Member, Mr. Speaker, I must tell him that, according to my information, the agreement between GM and Toyota is a private one. It is not part of any negotiation between the American government and Japan. This is strictly a private company, and for our part, we shall stress the need for an increased Japanese contribution to the Canadian economy. We shall certainly do so. However, this will be done in the context of our negotiations. I do not believe that it is wise to make threats without reason, especially when we announce them in advance, as the Hon. Member has suggested.
